newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia steps up fight against vodka import chaos.
newsitem.headline: Russia steps up fight against vodka import chaos.

text.p: Russia plans to tighten its grip on still unruly liquor imports and sales, primarily by licensing importers and making them pay duty up front, officials at the State Customs committee said on Thursday.

"We discussed tightening control over issuing licences to alcohol importers and several other measures to get a better grip on this important market," said one official, who declined to be named, after a meeting of CIS customs services.
He said Russia's customs committee would present its proposals to the government in two weeks.
These would also include 100 percent pre-payment of excise duties for imported alcohol, which the official said would guarantee higher quality imports.

Russian vodka producers hailed the move, saying they hoped it would introduce more order into the present chaotic state of the market, flooded by cheap imports and fake brands, allowing the state and legitimate producers to cash in on Russia's traditional strong drink.
"Everyone needs order on this market -- the state, producers and even importers themselves," said Vladimir Yarmosh, head of Rosalko vodka and alcohol producers' association.

"Our Russian folk are getting poisoned with bad vodka from abroad and from the local moonshine industry. This has to be stopped," Yarmosh said, adding that more than a half of all vodka sold in Russia was counterfeit, while Russia's share of the legal domestic vodka market was less than 50 percent.
Earlier this year the government introduced 1997 import quotas of 100 million litres of strong liquors and 10 million litres of ethanol.
The drastic import quotas are effective from January 1, 1997 and are aimed at protecting domestic producers.
"This is exactly what we wanted, the other thing to do is to re-issue licences for importers so that they cannot slip from under state control," he added.
However, the quotas ran into trouble with the International Monetary Fund, which voiced concern over the restrictions.
Customs officials said the new licensing rules and pre-payments could squeeze small importers out of the market, leaving bigger, law-abiding and more controllable structures to do business.
Producers said that famous foreign brands which are normally imported legally would face no limitations as they represent just two or three percent of total consumption.
"They don't have to worry there abroad. All their good whiskies and gins and vodkas will make it to the Russian shops and to the tables of those who love that stuff," Yarmosh said.
In the Soviet times the state used to receive up to one-third of its overall profits from vodka sales, but this share has fallen to only two percent over the past few years.

Experts have estimated average annual imports of vodka and ethanol at 1.27 billion litres (280 million gallons). Russia can produce up to 2.6 to 2.7 billion litres of vodka a year but the industry is working at about 30 percent capacity.
Producers suggested that 10 million litres of vodka from Ukraine and another 5 million from other former Soviet republics would be allowed under the 100 million litre import quota.
"But order is yet to return on our market. It is not going to happen overnight, it will take years," Yarmosh said.
